questions.q: Which table row correctly contrasts ANCA vasculitis with immune-complex mediated vasculitis?
opts: ANCA positive with deposits negative versus ANCA negative with deposits present
Granuloma always absent in ANCA and always present in immune-complex disease
Skin lesions absent in ANCA and absent in immune-complex disease
questions.exp: The comparison table shows ANCA vasculitis is ANCA positive with immune-complex deposits negative, while immune-complex mediated vasculitis is ANCA negative with deposits present. (Book p509)

questions.q: Which biopsy pattern is printed for immune-complex mediated vasculitis?
opts: Granuloma with giant cells in all cases
No skin lesion and no deposits
Leukocytoclasis with fragmented neutrophils and neutrophilic debris
Necrotizing inflammation with neutrophils and fibrinoid necrosis only
questions.exp: The immune-complex mediated biopsy row lists leukocytoclasis with fragmented neutrophils/neutrophilic debris. (Book p509)

questions.q: Which primary immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitides are listed?
opts: Behcet disease and Cogan syndrome only
HSP, cryoglobulinemia-associated vasculitis, HUV with anti-C1q positive and Goodpasture syndrome
questions.exp: Primary immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis list includes HSP, CAV, HUV with anti-C1q positivity and Goodpasture syndrome. (Book p509)

questions.q: Which secondary immune-complex mediated vasculitis causes are printed?
questions.exp: Secondary immune-complex mediated vasculitis is listed under SLE, RA, drugs and infections. (Book p509)

questions.q: Single-organ immune-complex vasculitis called cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis is also known as what?
questions.exp: Single-organ vasculitis is cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, involving only skin and AKA hypersensitive vasculitis. (Book p509)

questions.q: What pathogenesis sequence is printed for immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis?
opts: T-cell mediated Th1 over Th17 inflammation alone
Small immune complexes not cleared by RES activate complement and recruit neutrophils in superficial capillary dermis
ANCA triggers PR3/MPO expression then no deposits
questions.exp: The pathogenesis diagram shows small immune complexes not effectively cleared by RES, leading to complement activation and neutrophil recruitment in small vessels of superficial capillary dermis. (Book p510)

questions.q: What is the most characteristic skin lesion in this pathogenesis diagram?
questions.exp: Cutaneous palpable purpura is explicitly labelled the most characteristic skin lesion. (Book p510)

questions.q: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is also called what?
questions.exp: The HSP section states AKA IgA vasculitis. (Book p510)

questions.q: A boy aged 5 has symmetrical non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura on extensor lower limbs and buttocks occurring in crops. Which source diagnosis is most likely?
questions.exp: HSP is most common in children around 5 years, boys; non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura in a child is HSP unless proven otherwise, symmetrical on extensor lower limbs especially buttocks and occurring in crops. (Book p510)

questions.q: How common are joint symptoms in HSP, and what mnemonic features are printed?
opts: In 70%; KLNNO features: knee predominant, large joint, migratory, non-deforming oligoarthritis
questions.exp: Joint involvement occurs in 70%, 15% initially present with joint symptoms, and features are KLNNO: knee predominant, large joint, migratory, non-deforming oligoarthritis. (Book p511)

questions.q: HSP abdominal angina is described as colicky pain. Which complication is marked most dangerous?
questions.exp: GIT involvement is 50%; complications include hemorrhage, bowel ischemia, scrotal swelling and intussusception, specifically ileoileal as most dangerous. (Book p511)

questions.q: Which renal statement is printed for HSP?
opts: Renal disease occurs in 20–50%, usually asymptomatic microhematuria, and adults risk type 2 RPGN, ESRD and high relapse
Renal disease is absent in adults
Renal disease is renal artery stenosis only
questions.exp: HSP renal involvement is 20–50%, with asymptomatic microhematuria; adults can have type 2 RPGN, ESRD risk and high relapse rate. (Book p511)

questions.q: Which ACR criterion is listed for HSP?
questions.exp: ACR criteria shown are palpable purpura, age at onset <20 years, bowel angina and biopsy with vessel wall granulocytes. (Book p511)

questions.q: What HSP management statement is printed?
opts: Supportive care because disease is self-limiting; steroids for severe joint/GIT symptoms or adult RPGN
Cyclophosphamide for all children from day one
questions.exp: Treatment is supportive care because HSP is self-limiting with no disease/recurrence treatment; steroids are for severe joint/GIT symptoms or adult HSP with RPGN. (Book p511)

questions.q: Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins with what temperature behavior?
opts: Dissolve in cold and precipitate at 37°C
Precipitate in cold and dissolve on rewarming
questions.exp: Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate in cold and dissolve on rewarming. (Book p512)

questions.q: A middle-aged elderly female has increased Ig production with immunoglobulins adhering to small vessels more than medium vessels. Which source condition fits?
questions.exp: Cryoglobulinemia pathogenesis shows increased production of immunoglobulins adhering to small vessel surfaces more than medium vessels and is seen in middle-aged elderly females. (Book p512)

questions.q: Which type-1 cryoglobulinemia row is correct?
opts: IgA deposits with age below 5 years
Monoclonal IgG/IgM kappa or lambda, RF negative, associated with multiple myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
Polyclonal IgG plus monoclonal IgM, RF positive, HCV 90%
Polyclonal IgG/IgM, RF positive, SLE only
questions.exp: Type 1 cryoglobulinemia is monoclonal IgG/IgM kappa or lambda, RF negative, with multiple myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia including IgM and hyperviscosity symptoms. (Book p512)

questions.q: Which type is mixed cryoglobulinemia and what is its key association?
opts: Types 1 and 2; associated only with PAN
Types 2 and 3; type 2 is associated with hepatitis C in 90%
questions.exp: Mixed cryoglobulinemia is type 2 plus type 3; type 2 is associated with hepatitis C in 90% and Sjogren/SLE. (Book p512)

questions.q: Which extrahepatic HCV manifestations are listed in the cryoglobulinemia note?
opts: Porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus
questions.exp: Extrahepatic HCV manifestations listed are porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus. (Book p512)

questions.q: Which clinical manifestation set belongs to cryoglobulinemia?
opts: Confluent non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, ulcers/gangrene from medium-vessel involvement when HCV positive, arthralgia, HCV GIT involvement and MPGN
Symmetrical crops of buttock purpura in young boys only
questions.exp: Cryoglobulinemia manifestations include non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, ulcers/gangrene due to medium-vessel involvement in HCV-positive disease, arthralgia similar to SLE, HCV GIT involvement and MPGN. (Book p512)

questions.q: How does the source distinguish neuropathy patterns in cryoglobulinemia?
opts: Mononeuritis multiplex is medium-vessel; small-fibre neuropathy is small-vessel
questions.exp: The neurology note states mononeuritis multiplex is medium vessel and small fibre neuropathy is small vessel. (Book p513)

questions.q: What are the three components of Meltzer triad of cryoglobulinemia?
opts: Oral ulcer, genital ulcer and uveitis
questions.exp: The triangle labels Meltzer triad as purpura, arthralgia and myalgia or weakness. (Book p513)

questions.q: Which investigation pattern is printed for cryoglobulinemia?
opts: ANA by immunofluorescence and high complement
MR angiography as best test for all cases
Direct immunofluorescence with IgG/IgM and cryocrit with low C3/C4
questions.exp: Investigations list direct immunofluorescence showing IgG/IgM and cryocrit with decreased C3/C4. (Book p513)

questions.q: How is type 1 high-IgM cryoglobulinemia treated in the printed flow?
questions.exp: The treatment branch for type 1 high IgM lists PLEX, steroid and cyclophosphamide. (Book p513)

questions.q: For type 2/3 cryoglobulinemia, what does the HCV branch direct?
opts: If HCV positive treat HCV; if HCV negative use rituximab
If HCV positive use no treatment; if negative use antiviral
Both positive and negative branches use acyclovir
questions.exp: For type 2/3, HCV positive leads to treating HCV; HCV negative leads to rituximab. (Book p513)

questions.q: Which malignancy risk is highlighted at the end of the cryoglobulinemia page?
opts: Increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma
Increased risk of conversion to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.exp: The bottom note states increased risk of conversion to DLBCL, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. (Book p513)

units.title: 1. Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis and HSP
units.guide:
ANCA versus immune-complex comparisons are followed by primary, secondary and single-organ categories.
The immune-complex pathogenesis diagram leads into HSP age, skin, joint, GIT, renal, criteria and management.
All thresholds and complication lists are kept in printed order.

units.title: 2. Cryoglobulinemia
units.guide:
Cryoglobulin temperature behavior and type table open the block.
Mixed cryoglobulinemia, HCV extrahepatic features and organ manifestations follow.
Neuropathy, Meltzer triad, investigation and type-based treatment close the chapter.
